questions.q: One main scale division of a Vernier calliper is equal to $1$ mm and the number of divisions on the Vernier scale is $10$. When both the jaws touch each other, the Vernier scale shifts to the left of zero of the main scale in such a way that $4^{th}$ Vernier division coincides with a division of the main scale. If this Vernier calliper measures the length of a wire to be $1$ cm, the actual length of the wire is :
questions.solution:
The least count (LC) of the Vernier calliper is given by:

$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1 \text{ mm}}{10} = 0.1 \text{ mm} = 0.01 \text{ cm}$

Since the zero of the Vernier scale shifts to the left of the zero of the main scale, the instrument has a negative zero error.

The zero error is calculated as:

$\text{Zero error} = -4 \times \text{LC} = -4 \times 0.01 \text{ cm} = -0.04 \text{ cm}$

The actual length of the wire is obtained by subtracting the zero error from the measured length:

$\text{Actual length} = \text{Measured length} - \text{Zero error}$

$\text{Actual length} = 1.00 \text{ cm} - (-0.04 \text{ cm}) = 1.04 \text{ cm}$

Answer: $1.04$ cm

questions.solution:
Given $20$ VSD $= 16$ MSD.

Least count $= 1$ MSD $- 0.8$ MSD $= 0.2$ MSD.

Converting to cm, Least count $= 0.02$ cm.

Answer: $0.02$ cm

questions.q: A plano-convex lens of unknown material and unknown focal length is given. With the help of a spherometer we can measure the
options: radius of curvature of the curved surface
questions.solution: A spherometer is a device that does just as the name suggests: it measures a sphere. But what exactly would you measure on a sphere? You could measure its diameter or the circumference of a great circle, the surface area, or the radius. But all of these measurements will change proportionally to the radius $R$ of the sphere. Any surface that is curved has a radius of curvature, the radius of the sphere that approximates the surface locally. Thus, a spherometer can measure the radius of curvature of an item such as a lens and curved mirrors that are spherical.

questions.q: Which of the following measurements require ‘index correction’ ?
options: Measurement of speed of sound using resonance tube
Measurement of resistance of a wire using meter bridge
Measurement of gravitational acceleration using simple pendulum
Measurement of focal length of lenses using optical bench
questions.solution:
In an optical bench experiment, the distance between the index marks on the uprights may not be exactly equal to the actual distance between the optical centre of the lens and the tip of the pin. This difference is known as index error.

To obtain the true distance, an index correction must be applied to the observed distance. Therefore, the measurement of the focal length of lenses using an optical bench requires index correction.

In contrast, the resonance tube and meter bridge experiments require 'end correction'.

Answer: Measurement of focal length of lenses using optical bench

Consider the diameter of a spherical object being measured with the help of a Vernier callipers. Suppose its 10 Vernier Scale Divisions (V.S.D.) are equal to its 9 Main Scale Divisions (M.S.D.) The least division in the M.S. is 0.1 cm and the zero of V.S. is at $\mathrm{x}=0.1 \mathrm{~cm}$ when the jaws of Vernier callipers are closed.
If the main scale reading for the diameter is $\mathrm{M}=5 \mathrm{~cm}$ and the number of coinciding vernier division is 8 , the measured diameter after zero error correction, is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& 10 \text{ V.S.D. }=9 \text{ M.S.D. } \\
& 1 \text{ M.S.D. }=0.1 \mathrm{ cm} \text{ (Given) } \\
& 1 \text{ V.S.D. }=0.9 \text{ M.S.D. } \\
& 1 \text{ V.S.D. }=0.9 \times 0.1 \mathrm{ cm} \\
& \therefore \text{ V.S.D. }=0.09 \mathrm{ cm} \\
& \text{ L.C. }=1 \text{ M.S.D. }-1 \text{ V.S.D. } \\
& =(0.1-0.09) \mathrm{cm} \\
& =0.01 \mathrm{ cm} \\
& \text{ Reading }=5.08 \mathrm{ cm} \\
& \text{ Positive zero error }=0.1 \mathrm{ cm} \text{ (Given) } \\
& \therefore \text{ Final Corrected reading }=(5.08-0.1) \mathrm{cm} \\
& =4.98 \mathrm{ cm}
\end{aligned}$

&

& =$\left($1-$\frac{(\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{l})}{\mathrm{n}}\right) \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}} \text{ MSD }$\\
& $\text{ Here, }$1 $\mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{cm}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad $\mathrm{LC}=\frac{\mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{n}} \times \frac{\mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{cm}=\frac{\mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{n}^2} \mathrm{~cm}$\\
&
\end{aligned}

Reason (R): The drift velocity of electrons in a metallic wire is very high.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

If assertion is true, but reason is false.
Assertion is false, reason is true
questions.solution:

- Reason (R): "The drift velocity of electrons in a metallic wire is very high." False drift velocity in conductors is actually very small (typically of the order of mm/s), not high.
Hence \(A\) is true and \(R\) is false \(\rightarrow\) option (3).

questions.q: The main scale of a vernier calliper has $m$ divisions per centimetre. It is given that $n$ divisions of the vernier scale coincide with $(n-1)$ divisions of the main scale. While measuring the length of a cylinder, the zero of the vernier scale lies just after the $k^{\text{th}}$ mark of the main scale, and the $p^{\text{th}}$ division of the vernier scale coincides with a main scale mark. The measured length of the cylinder is
questions.solution:
The length of one main scale division is:
$1 \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{1}{m} \text{ cm}$

From the coincidence condition:
$n \text{ VSD} = (n-1) \text{ MSD}$
$\Rightarrow 1 \text{ VSD} = \dfrac{n-1}{n} \text{ MSD}$

The Least Count (LC) is:
$\text{LC} = 1 \text{ MSD} - 1 \text{ VSD} = \dfrac{1}{n} \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{1}{mn} \text{ cm}$

The total measured length is the sum of the Main Scale Reading (MSR) and the Vernier Scale Reading (VSR):
$\text{MSR} = k \times 1 \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{k}{m} \text{ cm}$
$\text{VSR} = p \times \text{LC} = \dfrac{p}{mn} \text{ cm}$

$\text{Total length} = \text{MSR} + \text{VSR} = \dfrac{k}{m} + \dfrac{p}{mn} = \dfrac{kn+p}{mn} \text{ cm}$

Answer: $\dfrac{kn+p}{mn} \text{ cm}$

questions.q: The circular main scale of a spectrometer is divided into half-degrees ($0.5^\circ$). It is observed that $30$ divisions of the vernier scale coincide exactly with $29$ divisions of the main scale. The least count of the spectrometer, in minutes, is:
questions.solution:
The value of one main scale division is $1\text{ MSD} = 0.5^\circ$.

Given that $30$ vernier scale divisions (VSD) coincide with $29$ main scale divisions (MSD), we can write:
$1\text{ VSD} = \dfrac{29}{30}\text{ MSD}$

The least count (LC) of the instrument is given by:
$\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}$
$\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - \dfrac{29}{30}\text{ MSD} = \dfrac{1}{30}\text{ MSD}$

Substitute the value of $1\text{ MSD}$:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1}{30} \times 0.5^\circ = \left(\dfrac{1}{60}\right)^\circ$

Since $1^\circ = 60\text{ minutes}$, we convert the least count into minutes:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1}{60} \times 60\text{ minutes} = 1\text{ minute}$

Answer: $1$

questions.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of $0.5\text{ mm}$ and $50$ divisions on its circular scale. When used to measure the thickness of a glass plate, the main scale reading is $2.0\text{ mm}$ and the total measured thickness is $2.34\text{ mm}$. questions.solution:
Least count (LC) of the screw gauge is given by:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of circular scale divisions}}$
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{0.5\text{ mm}}{50} = 0.01\text{ mm}$

The total reading is given by the formula:
$\text{Total Reading} = \text{Main Scale Reading (MSR)} + (\text{Circular Scale Reading (CSR)} \times \text{LC})$

Substituting the given values:
$2.34\text{ mm} = 2.0\text{ mm} + (\text{CSR} \times 0.01\text{ mm})$
$0.34\text{ mm} = \text{CSR} \times 0.01\text{ mm}$

$\text{CSR} = \dfrac{0.34}{0.01} = 34$

The coinciding division on the circular scale is $34$.

Answer: $34$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a standard Vernier calliper ($1$ main scale division $= 1$ mm, $10$ Vernier scale divisions $= 9$ main scale divisions), if the zero of the Vernier scale lies to the left of the main scale zero and the $4^{\text{th}}$ Vernier division coincides with a main scale division, the zero error is $-0.6$ mm.

Reason (R): For a negative zero error, the magnitude of the error is calculated as $(n \times \text{LC})$, where $n$ is the number of the coinciding Vernier division and $\text{LC}$ is the least count.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For a standard Vernier calliper, the least count (LC) is:

$\text{LC} = 1 \text{ MSD} - 1 \text{ VSD} = 1 \text{ mm} - 0.9 \text{ mm} = 0.1 \text{ mm}$

When the zero of the Vernier scale lies to the left of the main scale zero, the instrument has a negative zero error. The magnitude of a negative zero error is given by $(N - n) \times \text{LC}$, where $N$ is the total number of Vernier divisions and $n$ is the coinciding division.

$\text{Zero error} = -(10 - 4) \times 0.1 \text{ mm} = -6 \times 0.1 \text{ mm} = -0.6 \text{ mm}$

Thus, Assertion (A) is correct.

Reason (R) states that the magnitude is calculated as $(n \times \text{LC})$, which is the formula for a positive zero error, not a negative zero error. Therefore, Reason (R) is incorrect.

Hence, (A) is correct but (R) is not correct.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

When measuring the diameter of a sphere, the zero of the vernier scale lies just after the $3.2$ cm mark on the main scale, and the $4^{\text{th}}$ division of the vernier scale exactly coincides with a main scale division. First, we determine the least count (LC) of the vernier callipers.

Since $1$ MSD $= 1$ mm, $1$ VSD $= 0.8$ mm.

The least count is:

LC $= 1$ MSD $- 1$ VSD $= 1$ mm $- 0.8$ mm $= 0.2$ mm

Converting the least count to cm:

LC $= 0.02$ cm

Now, we calculate the total reading for the diameter of the sphere.

Main Scale Reading (MSR) $= 3.2$ cm

Vernier Scale Reading (VSR) $= 4$

Total Reading $= \text{MSR} + (\text{VSR} \times \text{LC})$

Total Reading $= 3.2 \text{ cm} + (4 \times 0.02 \text{ cm}) = 3.2 \text{ cm} + 0.08 \text{ cm} = 3.28 \text{ cm}$

Answer: $3.28$ cm

questions.q: A screw gauge has a pitch of $1\text{ mm}$ and $100$ divisions on its circular scale. questions.solution:
Least count (LC) of the screw gauge is:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of circular scale divisions}}$
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1\text{ mm}}{100} = 0.01\text{ mm}$

Since the zero of the circular scale is above the reference line when the jaws are closed, the screw gauge has a negative zero error.
$\text{Zero error} = -4 \times 0.01\text{ mm} = -0.04\text{ mm}$

The observed reading for the wire's diameter is:
$\text{Observed Reading} = \text{MSR} + (\text{CSR} \times \text{LC})$
$\text{Observed Reading} = 2\text{ mm} + (45 \times 0.01\text{ mm}) = 2.45\text{ mm}$

The true reading is obtained by subtracting the zero error from the observed reading:
$\text{True Reading} = \text{Observed Reading} - \text{Zero error}$
$\text{True Reading} = 2.45\text{ mm} - (-0.04\text{ mm}) = 2.49\text{ mm}$

Answer: $2.49\text{ mm}$

questions.q: To convert an angle measured in radians into seconds of arc, the value in radians must be multiplied by which of the following exact factors?
questions.solution:
We know the relationship between radians and degrees is $\pi \text{ rad} = 180^\circ$.

Therefore, $1 \text{ rad} = \dfrac{180}{\pi} \text{ degrees}$.

Since $1^\circ = 60'$ (minutes of arc) and $1' = 60''$ (seconds of arc), we have $1^\circ = 3600''$.

Substituting this into the radian conversion gives $1 \text{ rad} = \dfrac{180}{\pi} \times 3600''$.

Thus, to convert an angle from radians to seconds of arc, the value must be multiplied by the factor $\dfrac{180 \times 3600}{\pi}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{180 \times 3600}{\pi}$

questions.q: A vernier callipers has a least count of $0.05$ mm. The main scale is marked in half millimetres (i.e., $1$ MSD $= 0.5$ mm). If the vernier scale has $50$ divisions in total, how many main scale divisions coincide exactly with these $50$ vernier scale divisions?
questions.solution:
The least count (LC) of a vernier callipers is given by the difference between the length of one main scale division (MSD) and one vernier scale division (VSD).

LC $= 1$ MSD $- 1$ VSD

Given that LC $= 0.05$ mm and $1$ MSD $= 0.5$ mm, we can find the length of $1$ VSD:

$0.05$ mm $= 0.5$ mm $- 1$ VSD

$1$ VSD $= 0.5$ mm $- 0.05$ mm $= 0.45$ mm

The total length of the vernier scale, which has $50$ divisions, is:

Length of $50$ VSD $= 50 \times 0.45$ mm $= 22.5$ mm

To find how many main scale divisions coincide with this length, we divide the total length of the vernier scale by the length of one main scale division:

Number of coinciding MSD $= \dfrac{22.5 \text{ mm}}{0.5 \text{ mm}} = 45$

Thus, $45$ main scale divisions coincide exactly with $50$ vernier scale divisions.

Answer: $45$

questions.q: A student uses a standard Vernier calliper ($1$ main scale division = $1$ mm, $10$ Vernier scale divisions = $9$ main scale divisions) which is known to have a negative zero error. The actual thickness of a glass slab is exactly $3.20$ cm. When measuring the slab, the main scale reads $3.1$ cm and the $7^{th}$ Vernier division coincides with a main scale division. Which Vernier division coincides with a main scale division when the jaws of the calliper are brought into contact?
questions.solution:
The least count (LC) of the standard Vernier calliper is:

$\text{LC} = 1 \text{ mm} - 0.9 \text{ mm} = 0.1 \text{ mm} = 0.01 \text{ cm}$

The observed reading during the measurement is:

$\text{Observed reading} = \text{MSR} + (\text{VSR} \times \text{LC}) = 3.1 \text{ cm} + (7 \times 0.01 \text{ cm}) = 3.17 \text{ cm}$

The relationship between actual thickness, observed reading, and zero error is:

$\text{Actual reading} = \text{Observed reading} - \text{Zero error}$

$3.20 \text{ cm} = 3.17 \text{ cm} - \text{Zero error}$

$\text{Zero error} = 3.17 \text{ cm} - 3.20 \text{ cm} = -0.03 \text{ cm}$

For a negative zero error, the zero of the Vernier scale is to the left of the main scale zero. The magnitude of the error is given by:

$\text{Zero error} = -(N - n) \times \text{LC}$

where $N$ is the total number of Vernier divisions ($10$) and $n$ is the coinciding division.

$-0.03 \text{ cm} = -(10 - n) \times 0.01 \text{ cm}$

$10 - n = 3 \implies n = 7$

Thus, the $7^{th}$ Vernier division coincides when the jaws are in contact.

Answer: $7^{th}$

Total reading = $\text{MSR} + \text{VSR} = 2.3\text{ cm} + 0.030\text{ cm} = 2.330\text{ cm}$.

questions.q: The main scale of a circular vernier instrument has $N$ divisions per degree. It is given that $V$ divisions of the vernier scale coincide with $(V-1)$ divisions of the main scale. The least count of the instrument in minutes is
questions.solution:
The main scale has $N$ divisions per degree. Therefore, the value of one main scale division (MSD) is:
$1 \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{1}{N} \text{ degrees}$

Since $1 \text{ degree} = 60 \text{ minutes}$, we can express $1 \text{ MSD}$ in minutes:
$1 \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{60}{N} \text{ minutes}$

It is given that $V$ divisions of the vernier scale coincide with $(V-1)$ divisions of the main scale:
$V \text{ VSD} = (V-1) \text{ MSD}$
$1 \text{ VSD} = \dfrac{V-1}{V} \text{ MSD}$

The least count (LC) is the difference between one MSD and one VSD:
$\text{LC} = 1 \text{ MSD} - 1 \text{ VSD}$
$\text{LC} = 1 \text{ MSD} - \dfrac{V-1}{V} \text{ MSD} = \dfrac{1}{V} \text{ MSD}$

Substituting the value of $1 \text{ MSD}$ in minutes:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1}{V} \times \left(\dfrac{60}{N}\right) \text{ minutes} = \dfrac{60}{NV} \text{ minutes}$

Answer: $\dfrac{60}{NV}$

questions.q: A telescope observes two points on a distant planet. The linear separation between the points is $\pi \times 10^6 \text{ m}$, and they subtend an angle of $6'$ (minutes of arc) at the telescope. The distance to the planet from the telescope is:
questions.solution:
The plane angle subtended by an arc of length $s$ at a distance $D$ is given by $\theta = \dfrac{s}{D}$, provided $\theta$ is measured in radians.

Given:

$s = \pi \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

$\theta = 6'$

First, convert the angle into radians:

$6' = \left(\dfrac{6}{60}\right)^\circ = 0.1^\circ$

$0.1^\circ = 0.1 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} \text{ rad} = \dfrac{\pi}{1800} \text{ rad}$

Now, calculate the distance $D$:

$D = \dfrac{s}{\theta} = \dfrac{\pi \times 10^6}{\dfrac{\pi}{1800}}$

$D = 1800 \times 10^6 \text{ m} = 1.8 \times 10^9 \text{ m}$

Answer: $1.8 \times 10^9 \text{ m}$

questions.q: The least count of a vernier callipers is given as $x$ mm. It is observed that $N$ divisions of its vernier scale coincide exactly with $(N-2)$ divisions of the main scale. The value of one main scale division ($1\text{ MSD}$) is:
questions.solution:
The least count (LC) of a vernier callipers is defined as:
$\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}$

Given the coincidence relation:
$N\text{ VSD} = (N-2)\text{ MSD}$
$1\text{ VSD} = \dfrac{N-2}{N}\text{ MSD}$

Substitute this into the least count formula:
$\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - \left(\dfrac{N-2}{N}\right)\text{ MSD}$
$\text{LC} = \left(1 - \dfrac{N-2}{N}\right)\text{ MSD}$
$\text{LC} = \left(\dfrac{N - N + 2}{N}\right)\text{ MSD} = \dfrac{2}{N}\text{ MSD}$

We are given that $\text{LC} = x$. Therefore:
$x = \dfrac{2}{N}\text{ MSD}$

Rearranging to find the value of $1\text{ MSD}$:
$1\text{ MSD} = \dfrac{Nx}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{Nx}{2}$

$\text{Number of divisions per cm} = \dfrac{1}{1 \text{ MSD}} = \dfrac{1}{NC}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{NC}$
